hints: Notice what the straight line graph is telling you, think about which gas law links $pV$ directly to $T$.
Recall that $pV = nRT$ only holds perfectly for an ideal gas, so ask yourself which listed gas is closest to ideal.
Compare size and intermolecular forces, the smallest non-polar molecule with the weakest attractions will deviate least and stay on the straight line longest.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the ideal gas graph**

This straight line through increasing $T$ is exactly what we expect for an ideal gas at fixed moles.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$pV = nRT$$
For fixed $n$, $pV$ is directly proportional to $T$, so a plot of $pV$ against $T$ is a straight line with gradient $nR$.

**Recall why real gases deviate**

Real gases only follow this line when intermolecular forces and molecular volume are negligible.

At low $T$ or high $p$, molecules are close together, attractions pull them in and the finite size matters, so the graph curves away from ideal.

**Pick the most ideal gas**

The most ideal gas has very small, light, non-polar molecules with only very weak London dispersion forces.

$\text{H}_2$ is tiny and non-polar with the weakest attractions, while $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HF}$ (polar, plus hydrogen bonding in $\text{HF}$) and the larger $\text{O}_2$ deviate much more easily. So hydrogen stays on the straight line over the widest range.

options.A: Correct. Hydrogen, $\text{H}_2$, is very small, light and non-polar with only extremely weak London forces. Its own molecular volume is negligible and attractions are minimal, so it behaves most like an ideal gas and follows $pV = nRT$ over the widest range of $T$ and $p$.
options.B: Hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, is polar with permanent dipole-dipole forces in addition to London forces. These significant attractions cause deviation from ideal behaviour much sooner than for $\text{H}_2$.
options.C: Hydrogen fluoride, $\text{HF}$, is strongly polar and forms hydrogen bonds, the strongest type of intermolecular force here. It deviates very strongly from ideal behaviour and can even associate, so it leaves the straight line quickly.
options.D: Oxygen, $\text{O}_2$, is non-polar but it is much larger and has many more electrons than $\text{H}_2$, so its London forces are stronger and its molecular volume is larger. It is more ideal than $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HF}$, but less ideal than $\text{H}_2$.
